summary: Provides test vectors for HMAC combined with the SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 hash functions, which implementers can use to check conformance. It also gives ASN.1 object identifiers and URIs so protocols can name these schemes. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This document gives the official names and known answers for four message authentication schemes: HMAC built on SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512. The names let protocols refer to a scheme, and the known answers let an implementer check that its code produces exactly the same results as everyone else's.

subtitle: Official names and known-answer test cases for HMAC with SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512.

tldr.problem: Protocols need unambiguous names for HMAC combined with the SHA-2 hash functions, and implementers need known-correct answers to check their code against.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC allocates ASN.1 object identifiers and algorithm URIs for the four schemes and lists seven test cases with keys, data and expected HMAC values.
tldr.outcome: An implementation that matches the published results should interoperate with other implementations. The RFC makes no claim about how secure the schemes are for any use.

today: RFC 4231 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the reference for these identifiers and test vectors.

sections.title: What This Document Provides
sections.content:
This document provides test vectors for four message authentication schemes: HMAC-SHA-224, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA-512. It also provides ASN.1 object identifiers and Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) that identify use of these schemes in protocols.

The identifiers are meant for protocols that use ASN.1 constructs, such as those built on Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME), and the URIs are meant for protocols based on XML constructs, such as those using XML Digital Signatures. The test vectors may be used for conformance testing.

One convention is defined here: the keyword SHOULD in this document is to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things are needed when a protocol uses a keyed hash: a name for the exact combination of hash and keying rule, and a way to check that an implementation computes it correctly. This document supplies both, for four combinations at once.

sections.title: The Four HMAC-SHA Schemes
sections.content:
Each scheme is the realization of the HMAC message authentication code from RFC 2104 using one of the SHA-2 hash functions. HMAC-SHA-224 uses SHA-224, HMAC-SHA-256 uses SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384 uses SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA-512 uses SHA-512. The hash functions themselves are described in the NIST Secure Hash Standard, FIPS 180-2.

The block size of the hash function matters for the test cases. It is 64 bytes for SHA-224 and SHA-256, and 128 bytes for SHA-384 and SHA-512. A key longer than the block size has to be hashed before it is used, and several test cases deliberately use keys or data larger than a block so that this path is exercised.
sections.plainLanguage: All four schemes use the same keying rule from RFC 2104 and differ only in the hash function inside it. The hash function works on blocks of data, and the block size is 64 bytes for SHA-224 and SHA-256 and 128 bytes for SHA-384 and SHA-512. That size decides when a long key has to be shortened before use.

sections.title: Scheme Identifiers: Object Identifiers and URIs
sections.content:
The ASN.1 object identifiers are allocated under rsadsi, which is {iso(1) member-body(2) us(840) rsadsi(113549)}. The branch digestAlgorithm is {rsadsi 2}, and the four schemes sit beneath it: id-hmacWithSHA224 as {digestAlgorithm 8}, id-hmacWithSHA256 as {digestAlgorithm 9}, id-hmacWithSHA384 as {digestAlgorithm 10} and id-hmacWithSHA512 as {digestAlgorithm 11}.

When the algorithm component of a value of ASN.1 type AlgorithmIdentifier identifies one of these schemes, the parameter component SHOULD be present but have type NULL.

Four URIs are also allocated, one for each scheme, in the PKCS #5 schema of RSA Security, ending in #hmac-sha-224, #hmac-sha-256, #hmac-sha-384 and #hmac-sha-512. As usual, when they are used in the context of XML-Signature, the ds:HMACOutputLength element may specify the truncated length of the scheme output.
sections.plainLanguage: Each scheme gets a numbered identifier in the ASN.1 directory of cryptographic algorithms, and a URI ending in the scheme name. When a protocol says which scheme it uses, the parameter field should be present and empty.

sections.title: The Seven Test Cases
sections.content:
Seven test cases follow, with keys, data and digests given in hex. Each case lists the expected output for all four schemes, so one implementation can check every scheme at once.

Test case 1 uses a 20-byte key of repeated 0b bytes and the data "Hi There". Test case 2 uses the key "Jefe", which is shorter than the length of the HMAC output, with the data "what do ya want for nothing?". Test case 3 uses a 20-byte key and 50 bytes of data, so that the combined length is larger than 64 bytes, the block size of SHA-224 and SHA-256. Test case 4 does the same with a 25-byte key.

Test case 5 tests truncation of the output to 128 bits. Test case 6 uses a 131-byte key, larger than the 128-byte block size of SHA-384 and SHA-512, and notes that the key has to be hashed first. Test case 7 uses that same size of key with data that is also larger than the block size, so that the key needs to be hashed before being used by the HMAC algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: Seven cases give a key, some data and the expected result for each of the four schemes. The cases cover a short key, a key and data that together exceed one block, a truncated result, and a key longer than the block size, which the algorithm hashes before use.

sections.title: Using the Vectors for Conformance
sections.content:
The test vectors in this document have been cross-verified by three independent implementations. An implementation that concurs with the results provided here should be interoperable with other similar implementations.

The test cases are derived from those in RFC 2202, which covers HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA-1, although the keys and data are slightly different. The document also thanks Jim Schaad and Brad Hards for assistance in verifying the results.
sections.plainLanguage: Three separate implementations produced the same results for these cases. If your implementation matches them, it will work with other implementations that follow this document.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document says it is intended to provide the identifications and test vectors for the four message authentication code schemes to the Internet community, and that no assertion of the security of these schemes for any particular use is intended. For the general security of the HMAC construction, the reader is referred to RFC 2104.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives names and test answers only. It makes no claim about how safe these schemes are for any particular job, and points to RFC 2104 for the security of the HMAC construction itself.
